notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design a parking lot: cars enter, get a ticket and a spot, and pay when leaving. In an LLD interview you first pin down what is in and out of scope, then say it out loud.

Functional (what we build):

  • Several spot sizes (bike, car, truck). A vehicle can use a spot of its size or bigger (a bike may use a car spot only if no bike spot is free).
  • park(plate, type) returns a ticket with the spot, or "full" for that size.
  • unpark(ticket) frees the spot and returns the fee. Fee is per started hour, with a rate per vehicle type.

Non-functional: pricing and spot choice must be swappable (open/closed), and two cars must never get the same spot.

Out of scope for the first 30 minutes: multiple floors, payment gateways, EV charging, reservations. Mention them in Follow-ups.

Worked example. 4 spots (1 bike, 2 car, 1 truck). A car enters at t=0 and leaves after 2 h 1 min. Started hours = ceil(2.0167) = 3. Car rate 30 per hour, so the fee is 90.

Industry examples. Airport and mall systems (Skidata, Flowbird) work exactly like this: a ticket, an entry sensor and a rate table; Indian FASTag lots skip the ticket and key on the plate.

Everyday analogy. A cloakroom: you hand something in, get a numbered token, and the attendant must never give two people the same hook.

Common interview traps.

  • Starting to code before asking about sizes, floors and pricing.
  • Forgetting the "full" case: park must be able to say no.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
Nouns in the requirements become classes:

  • Spot: id, the biggest vehicle it fits, and a taken flag.
  • Ticket: id, the spot, the plate, entry time. It is the proof of parking.
  • VehicleType: an enum ordered by size, so fits is just ordinal comparison.
  • ParkingLot: the facade. It holds spots and active tickets and exposes park and unpark.
  • SpotStrategy and PricingStrategy: the two parts that change, so they are interfaces.

Why the ticket holds the spot and not just an id. unpark becomes O(1): no search over all spots. This is the data-structure choice interviewers watch for.

Decision gravity. Splitting strategies out is cheap to do now and reversible; hard-coding fee math inside ParkingLot makes "add weekend pricing" a risky edit later. Using an enum for sizes is a mild one-way door: adding "EV" or "handicapped" spots later means a second dimension (spot attributes), not a new enum value.

Everyday analogy. The ticket is the cloakroom token; the strategies are the attendant's rulebook and the price list pinned on the wall.

Common interview traps.

  • Making Vehicle a class hierarchy (Car, Bike, Truck) when only the size matters. An enum is enough until behaviour differs.
  • Searching all spots to find the car on exit.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
+--------------------+        +------------------+
 | ParkingLot         |------->| SpotStrategy     |<|-- NearestFreeSpot
 |  spots: List<Spot> |        | pick(spots, v)   |
 |  active: Map<id,T> |        +------------------+
 |  park(plate, v)    |        +------------------+
 |  unpark(id, now)   |------->| PricingStrategy  |<|-- HourlyPricing
 +--------------------+        | fee(v, duration) |
        | has many             +------------------+
        v
 +--------------+    1   issued for   1  +----------------+
 | Spot         |<-----------------------| Ticket         |
 |  id, type    |                        |  id, spot,     |
 |  taken(atomic)|                       |  plate, entry  |
 +--------------+                        +----------------+
 enum VehicleType { BIKE, CAR, TRUCK }   (ordered by size)

Read it as: ParkingLot owns spots and tickets, and delegates two decisions (which spot, how much) to strategies. A subclass SafeParkingLot (Concurrency section) changes only how state is protected.

Common interview traps.

  • Drawing arrows without saying what they mean (owns, uses, inherits).
  • Putting fee() on Ticket: then pricing cannot vary without touching the ticket.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Strategy (SpotStrategy, PricingStrategy). Why: spot choice (nearest, tightest fit, near the lift) and pricing (hourly, daily cap, weekend) change independently of the lot. Alternative: if/else on a mode flag, which breaks open/closed. Reversible and cheap.
  • Facade (ParkingLot). Callers see two methods, not spots and tickets. Alternative: expose the lists, which leaks internals.
  • Factory (optional). A ParkingLotFactory.build(config) that creates spots from a floor plan. Skip it unless asked; naming it is enough.
  • Singleton? Avoid. Many answers make the lot a Singleton. That hurts tests (shared state) and multi-lot support. Pass it in by constructor instead.

Industry examples. Spring's PlatformTransactionManager and Java's Comparator are Strategy in the wild; Android's RecyclerView.LayoutManager is a Strategy chosen by the app.

Everyday analogy. A taxi meter: the meter (lot) stays the same, the tariff card (strategy) changes by city.

Common interview traps.

  • Naming patterns without tying each to a real change you expect.
  • Using Singleton and then being unable to unit test.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
Java (compiled and run with JDK 21). It is a single file: copy it into Demo.java together with the Run and test section.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.concurrent.*;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.*;

enum VehicleType { BIKE, CAR, TRUCK }

class Spot {
    final int id;
    final VehicleType type;           // the biggest vehicle this spot fits
    final AtomicBoolean taken = new AtomicBoolean(false);
    Spot(int id, VehicleType type) { this.id = id; this.type = type; }
    boolean fits(VehicleType v) { return v.ordinal() <= type.ordinal(); }
}

class Ticket {
    final String id; final Spot spot; final String plate; final long entryMs;
    Ticket(String id, Spot spot, String plate, long entryMs) {
        this.id = id; this.spot = spot; this.plate = plate; this.entryMs = entryMs;
    }
}

interface SpotStrategy { Optional<Spot> pick(List<Spot> spots, VehicleType v); }

class NearestFreeSpot implements SpotStrategy {           // spots are sorted by distance to the gate
    public Optional<Spot> pick(List<Spot> spots, VehicleType v) {
        Spot best = null;
        for (Spot s : spots)
            if (!s.taken.get() && s.fits(v) && (best == null || s.type.ordinal() < best.type.ordinal()))
                best = s;                                  // tightest fit wins, first by distance on ties
        return Optional.ofNullable(best);
    }
}

interface PricingStrategy { long fee(VehicleType v, long durationMs); }

class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy {
    private final Map<VehicleType, Long> perHour = Map.of(
        VehicleType.BIKE, 10L, VehicleType.CAR, 30L, VehicleType.TRUCK, 80L);
    public long fee(VehicleType v, long ms) {
        long hours = Math.max(1, (ms + 3_599_999) / 3_600_000);   // ceil, minimum 1 hour
        return hours * perHour.get(v);
    }
}

class ParkingLot {
    protected final List<Spot> spots;
    protected final SpotStrategy strategy;
    protected final PricingStrategy pricing;
    protected final Map<String, Ticket> active = new HashMap<>();
    protected final Map<String, VehicleType> kind = new HashMap<>();
    protected int seq = 0;

    ParkingLot(List<Spot> spots, SpotStrategy s, PricingStrategy p) {
        this.spots = spots; this.strategy = s; this.pricing = p;
    }

    Optional<Ticket> park(String plate, VehicleType v, long nowMs) {
        Optional<Spot> pick = strategy.pick(spots, v);
        if (pick.isEmpty()) return Optional.empty();           // lot full for this size
        Spot s = pick.get();
        s.taken.set(true);
        Ticket t = new Ticket("T" + (++seq), s, plate, nowMs);
        active.put(t.id, t); kind.put(t.id, v);
        return Optional.of(t);
    }

    long unpark(String ticketId, long nowMs) {
        Ticket t = active.remove(ticketId);
        if (t == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown ticket " + ticketId);
        t.spot.taken.set(false);
        return pricing.fee(kind.remove(ticketId), nowMs - t.entryMs);
    }
}

The same core in Kotlin (translated by hand, not compiled in this session):

enum class VehicleType { BIKE, CAR, TRUCK }

class Spot(val id: Int, val type: VehicleType) {
    val taken = java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean(false)
    fun fits(v: VehicleType) = v.ordinal <= type.ordinal
}
class Ticket(val id: String, val spot: Spot, val plate: String, val entryMs: Long, val kind: VehicleType)

interface PricingStrategy { fun fee(v: VehicleType, durationMs: Long): Long }
class HourlyPricing : PricingStrategy {
    private val perHour = mapOf(VehicleType.BIKE to 10L, VehicleType.CAR to 30L, VehicleType.TRUCK to 80L)
    override fun fee(v: VehicleType, durationMs: Long) =
        maxOf(1L, (durationMs + 3_599_999) / 3_600_000) * perHour.getValue(v)
}

class ParkingLot(private val spots: List<Spot>, private val pricing: PricingStrategy) {
    private val live = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, Ticket>()
    private val ids = java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger()

    fun park(plate: String, v: VehicleType, now: Long): Ticket? {
        while (true) {
            val s = spots.filter { !it.taken.get() && it.fits(v) }
                .minByOrNull { it.type.ordinal } ?: return null          // tightest fit, nearest first
            if (s.taken.compareAndSet(false, true)) {
                val t = Ticket("T${ids.incrementAndGet()}", s, plate, now, v)
                live[t.id] = t
                return t
            }
        }
    }

    fun unpark(id: String, now: Long): Long {
        val t = live.remove(id) ?: error("unknown ticket $id")
        val fee = pricing.fee(t.kind, now - t.entryMs)
        t.spot.taken.set(false)
        return fee
    }
}

Notes on choices: taken is an AtomicBoolean from the start so the thread-safe version can reuse Spot. NearestFreeSpot prefers the tightest fit so a bike does not waste a truck spot. Fee uses integer ceil math (ms + 3_599_999) / 3_600_000 to avoid floating point.

Common interview traps.

  • Using double for money; use integer minor units.
  • Letting a bike take a truck spot while a bike spot is free.

notes.title: Run and test
notes.html:
public class Demo {
    static List<Spot> spots() {
        return new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Spot(1, VehicleType.BIKE), new Spot(2, VehicleType.CAR),
            new Spot(3, VehicleType.CAR), new Spot(4, VehicleType.TRUCK)));
    }
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ParkingLot lot = new ParkingLot(spots(), new NearestFreeSpot(), new HourlyPricing());
        Ticket t = lot.park("KA01", VehicleType.CAR, 0).get();
        System.out.println("car got spot " + t.spot.id);                       // 2
        System.out.println("bike got spot " + lot.park("KA02", VehicleType.BIKE, 0).get().spot.id); // 1
        long fee = lot.unpark(t.id, 2 * 3_600_000L + 60_000);                  // 2h01m -> 3 billable hours
        System.out.println("fee = " + fee);                                    // 90
        lot.park("KA03", VehicleType.CAR, 0); lot.park("KA04", VehicleType.CAR, 0);
        System.out.println("truck fits? " + lot.park("KA05", VehicleType.TRUCK, 0).isPresent()); // true: the TRUCK spot (4) is still free

        // concurrency: 5 spots, 40 threads, exactly 5 may win
        List<Spot> five = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) five.add(new Spot(i, VehicleType.CAR));
        ParkingLot safe = new SafeParkingLot(five, new NearestFreeSpot(), new HourlyPricing());
        ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16);
        AtomicInteger wins = new AtomicInteger();
        CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1);
        List<Future<?>> fs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) { final int n = i;
            fs.add(ex.submit(() -> { go.await(); if (safe.park("P" + n, VehicleType.CAR, 0).isPresent()) wins.incrementAndGet(); return null; })); }
        go.countDown();
        for (Future<?> f : fs) f.get();
        ex.shutdown();
        System.out.println("safe wins = " + wins.get());                       // 5
    }
}

Actual output from javac Demo.java && java Demo:

car got spot 2
bike got spot 1
fee = 90
truck fits? true
safe wins = 5

The last line is the concurrency check: 40 threads fight for 5 spots and exactly 5 win.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "I would test it" without naming cases: full lot, exact hour boundary, unknown ticket, double exit.
  • Tests that depend on the real clock; pass time in as a parameter, as here.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
The race. ParkingLot.park does check-then-act: pick a free spot, then mark it taken. Two gates running at once can both pick spot 2, so two cars get one spot. HashMap and ++seq are also unsafe.

Fix options, with gravity.

  1. One big synchronized on park and unpark. Simple and correct; throughput limited to one entry at a time, which is fine for one lot (a gate handles maybe 1 car every 5 s). Reversible.
  2. Compare-and-set on the spot (below). Lock-free claim; many gates proceed in parallel.
  3. A database row lock or unique constraint (UPDATE spots SET taken=1 WHERE id=? AND taken=0, check rows updated). Needed when many servers run the lot service.

The thread-safe version uses option 2: the strategy only suggests a spot, then compareAndSet(false, true) decides who really gets it, and the loser retries with the next best.

class SafeParkingLot extends ParkingLot {
    private final AtomicInteger ids = new AtomicInteger();
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Ticket> live = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, VehicleType> kinds = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    SafeParkingLot(List<Spot> spots, SpotStrategy s, PricingStrategy p) { super(spots, s, p); }

    @Override Optional<Ticket> park(String plate, VehicleType v, long nowMs) {
        while (true) {                                          // retry if another thread grabs our pick
            Optional<Spot> pick = strategy.pick(spots, v);
            if (pick.isEmpty()) return Optional.empty();
            Spot s = pick.get();
            if (s.taken.compareAndSet(false, true)) {           // atomic claim: only one thread wins
                Ticket t = new Ticket("T" + ids.incrementAndGet(), s, plate, nowMs);
                live.put(t.id, t); kinds.put(t.id, v);
                return Optional.of(t);
            }
        }
    }

    @Override long unpark(String ticketId, long nowMs) {
        Ticket t = live.remove(ticketId);                       // remove is atomic: double exit fails
        if (t == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown ticket " + ticketId);
        long fee = pricing.fee(kinds.remove(ticketId), nowMs - t.entryMs);
        t.spot.taken.set(false);                                // free the spot last
        return fee;
    }
}

Production detail. Free the spot after computing the fee and removing the ticket, and remove from the map atomically, so a double scan of one ticket at the exit cannot charge or free twice. Symptom of the bug in production: two cars with the same spot on the display board, found by comparing active ticket count to taken-spot count.

Everyday analogy. Two people reaching for the last seat: only the one whose hand lands first (the CAS) sits; the other looks for another seat.

Common interview traps.

  • Marking park as synchronized but leaving unpark unsynchronized.
  • Using volatile boolean for the flag: visibility without atomicity does not stop double booking.
  • Locking in the strategy instead of at the claim point.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Multiple floors. Add Floor holding spots; the lot asks each floor in order, or the strategy picks floor by availability. Mostly an extension of SpotStrategy.
  • Display board "free spots per type". Keep a counter per type updated on park/unpark (LongAdder) instead of scanning.
  • Lost ticket / daily cap. New PricingStrategy implementations; no change to the lot.
  • Many entrances on many servers. State moves to a database; use the row-level claim from Concurrency option 3.
  • Reservations. Add a RESERVED state to the spot with an expiry.
  • Find my car. Index plate to ticket with a second map.

Common interview traps.

  • Re-designing everything for each follow-up instead of naming which single class changes.
  • Not saying what you would give up (simplicity) when adding scale.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Entities: Spot, Ticket, ParkingLot, enum VehicleType; strategies for spot choice and price.
  • Strategy pattern isolates what changes (rules, price); Facade keeps the API to two methods; avoid Singleton.
  • Ticket holds its spot so exit is O(1); fee uses integer ceil hours.
  • Race: check-then-act on a spot. Fix with CAS on the spot (or a DB conditional update across servers); remove tickets atomically.
  • Follow-ups map to one class each: floors, display counters, new pricing, reservations.

questions.promptHtml: In a parking lot design, why does the Ticket hold a reference to its Spot instead of just a spot id? And why is VehicleType an enum rather than a Car/Bike/Truck class hierarchy?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They watch whether you pick data structures for the hot path (exit) and whether you avoid class hierarchies that carry no behaviour.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If the ticket holds the spot, unpark is O(1): look up the ticket by id in a map, flip taken on the spot it points to. With only an id I would scan all spots or keep a second map. The enum is enough because only the size matters; a Car class with no different behaviour is noise. I would introduce subclasses only when vehicles behave differently.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Entry builds the ticket once, exit reads it once, so the ticket is the proof of parking and the index at the same time.

park:   strategy.pick(spots, v) -> Spot s -> Ticket(id, s, plate, entry) -> active[id] = ticket
unpark: active.remove(id)       -> ticket  -> ticket.spot.taken = false  -> fee(kind, now-entry)

The enum is ordered by size (BIKE < CAR < TRUCK), so spot.fits(v) is v.ordinal() <= spot.type.ordinal(). This is a mild one-way door: when "EV" or "handicapped" spots arrive, size is no longer the only dimension and you add spot attributes, not one more enum value.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Searching every spot on exit to find the car.
  • Making Vehicle a hierarchy "because the nouns are there".
  • Putting fee() on Ticket, so pricing cannot vary.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the ticket is lost? -> Look up by plate through a second index plate -> ticket, and charge a lost-ticket PricingStrategy.
  2. Why not store the entry time on the spot? -> A spot is reused; the entry time belongs to one stay, which is what the ticket models.
  3. When would a Vehicle class be justified? -> When behaviour differs, for example a truck needing two adjacent spots or an EV needing a charger check.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "for speed". The senior names the O(1) exit, the ordering trick on the enum, and states which decision is reversible (strategies) and which is a one-way door (enum for size).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A lot system that scanned all 4,000 spots per exit made the exit barrier lag at rush hour; indexing by ticket removed the scan.

questions.subtopic: Strategy, Facade, and why not Singleton
questions.promptHtml: Which patterns do you use in the parking lot and what real change does each one absorb? Why do many answers make ParkingLot a Singleton and why is that a problem?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: To separate people who name patterns from people who tie each pattern to a change they expect.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Strategy for spot choice and for pricing, because both change independently of the lot (nearest, tightest fit, weekend rates). Facade because callers should see only park and unpark, not spots and tickets. I avoid Singleton: it hides shared state, makes tests leak into each other and blocks multiple lots. I pass the lot in through the constructor.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Client -> ParkingLot (Facade) -> SpotStrategy   (which spot?)
                              -> PricingStrategy (how much?)

Alternative for Strategy is if/else on a mode flag, which means every new rule edits ParkingLot and breaks open/closed. Strategy is cheap and reversible. A Factory that builds spots from a floor plan is optional; naming it is enough.

Singleton problems: a static getInstance() is a global variable, so test A leaves cars parked for test B; two lots (two buildings) cannot coexist; and you cannot swap in a fake pricing.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Naming five patterns with no change each absorbs.
  • Singleton, then "how do I unit test it?" with no answer.
  • Leaking the List<Spot> through the facade.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. If you must have one lot per process, how? -> Create it once at startup (main or a DI container) and inject it; one instance by wiring, not by static.
  2. Strategy vs State? -> Strategy: the caller picks the algorithm. State: the object switches its own behaviour as it moves between states.
  3. Where would a Factory earn its place? -> Building 12 floors of spots from a config file or database rows.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists patterns. The senior says which are reversible, which one the interviewer's follow-ups will hit (pricing), and refuses Singleton with test reasons.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A global lot singleton made integration tests order-dependent; fixing it by constructor injection removed the flakiness.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate "made the lot thread-safe". Two entry gates and one exit gate call it from different threads. In the pilot, the display board occasionally shows 2 cars on spot 7.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class ParkingLot {
    private final List<Spot> spots; private final SpotStrategy strategy;
    private final Map<String, Ticket> active = new HashMap<>();
    private int seq = 0;

    synchronized Optional<Ticket> park(String plate, VehicleType v, long now) {
        Optional<Spot> pick = strategy.pick(spots, v);
        if (pick.isEmpty()) return Optional.empty();
        pick.get().taken.set(true);
        Ticket t = new Ticket("T" + (++seq), pick.get(), plate, now);
        active.put(t.id, t);
        return Optional.of(t);
    }

    long unpark(String id, long now) {            // not synchronized
        Ticket t = active.remove(id);
        t.spot.taken.set(false);
        return fee(t, now);
    }
}
class ParkingLot(private val spots: List<Spot>, private val strategy: SpotStrategy) {
    private val active = HashMap<String, Ticket>()
    private var seq = 0

    @Synchronized fun park(plate: String, v: VehicleType, now: Long): Ticket? {
        val s = strategy.pick(spots, v) ?: return null
        s.taken.set(true)
        return Ticket("T${++seq}", s, plate, now).also { active[it.id] = it }
    }

    fun unpark(id: String, now: Long): Long {     // not synchronized
        val t = active.remove(id)!!
        t.spot.taken.set(false)
        return fee(t, now)
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find every concurrency bug and fix it without making the whole lot a single global lock bottleneck.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add synchronized to unpark too." That fixes the HashMap, but the two-cars-one-spot symptom came from somewhere else, and the answer cannot say which line produced it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are park callers on one JVM? (yes, so no DB needed). Is the board derived from taken or from active? What is the exit rate, so I know if a lock is acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make unpark synchronized too: a one-line patch that stops map corruption now.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) park is synchronized but unpark mutates active and taken with no lock: HashMap race, and the park lock does not exclude it. (b) Double scan of one ticket at exit: second call gets null and throws NPE, or frees a spot that was already re-assigned. (c) A second lot instance created by mistake.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare active.size() to the count of taken==true spots in a periodic audit; log ticket id and thread at claim and release; run a stress test with 40 threads on 5 spots and assert exactly 5 wins.
  5. Root cause: Locking is per method, not per invariant. The invariant is "a spot is taken by at most one live ticket", and exit changes the same state under another lock (none).
  6. Fix: Short term: synchronize both. Long term: claim the spot with AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true) after the strategy only suggests it, retry on loss, use ConcurrentHashMap, and free the spot last, after active.remove(id) returned non-null so a double exit is rejected.
  7. Prevention: A concurrency test in CI (latch, 40 threads, 5 spots), and an audit metric takenSpots - activeTickets that must be 0.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use volatile on the flag: it gives visibility, not atomic check-then-act. One big lock is fine for one lot (a gate handles maybe a car every few seconds); CAS buys parallelism that this scale barely needs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why free the spot last? -> If freed first, another gate can take it while the first exit still computes the fee from the old ticket; also a failing fee call would leak a freed spot.
  • Is ids.incrementAndGet() enough for ticket ids across restarts? -> No; use a persisted sequence or UUID.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An exit gate retried a scan after a network blip. The unsynchronized exit freed a spot twice, and a new car was parked on it between the two frees. Symptom: taken count 1 lower than active tickets, for days.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds synchronized to one more method with no invariant stated.
  • Hire: finds the unsynchronized exit and the double-exit hazard, fixes both.
  • Strong hire: states the invariant, uses CAS plus atomic map removal, gives the audit metric and the stress test.

questions.contextHtml:
Support tickets say customers are charged 0 for stays under an hour and are undercharged on stays like 2h10m. Car rate is 30 per hour. Finance wants "per started hour, minimum one hour".

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
long fee(VehicleType v, long durationMs) {
    long hours = durationMs / 3_600_000;           // integer division
    return hours * perHour.get(v);
}
fun fee(v: VehicleType, durationMs: Long): Long {
    val hours = durationMs / 3_600_000
    return hours * perHour.getValue(v)
}

A second engineer proposes Math.ceil(durationMs / 3_600_000.0) * rate as a double.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, what does the correct computation look like, and what would you test?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Math.ceil" with doubles, no minimum-one-hour rule, and no tests at the boundaries.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a grace period allowed (first 10 minutes free)? Is exactly 2h00m two hours or three? Currency minor unit (paise, cents)? Daylight saving or time zones, or do we use epoch millis?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship the integer ceil fix and list the affected tickets for a refund or top-up decision with finance.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Integer division truncates (0 hours for 59 minutes; 2 hours for 2h59m); no minimum-hour rule; the double-based fix would introduce rounding noise and money in floats.
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit tests at 0 ms, 1 ms, 3_599_999, 3_600_000, 3_600_001, 2h01m (expected 90 for a car).
  5. Root cause: Wrong rounding direction for a "per started hour" rule.
  6. Fix: max(1, (ms + 3_599_999) / 3_600_000) * rate in long arithmetic; no floating point.
  7. Prevention: Table-driven boundary tests; money always in minor units as long; pricing behind PricingStrategy so rule changes do not touch the lot.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use double for money or BigDecimal just for integer hours; I would not compute with the wall clock inside the strategy, I pass the duration in.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Add a daily cap of 400? -> New PricingStrategy wrapping hourly: min(hourly, cap * days); the lot does not change.
  • Stay of 25 days? -> long is fine: 25 days is about 2.2e9 ms, which overflows int (max about 2.1e9), so the type matters.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A lot charged 0 for the first hour for a quarter before anyone noticed because the "free hour" was an unintended side effect of truncation.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swaps in Math.ceil on doubles and stops.
  • Hire: integer ceil with minimum one hour and boundary tests.
  • Strong hire: also raises grace period, overflow, and money-in-minor-units, and keeps it a pluggable strategy.

questions.contextHtml: The lot works with enum VehicleType { BIKE, CAR, TRUCK } ordered by size. Product now wants EV spots with chargers (15 of 400 spots), handicapped-accessible spots (20 of 400) and a rule that an EV may use a normal car spot but a non-EV car may not take an EV spot unless the lot is over 95 percent full.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, which do not, and what do you do about the enum?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds EV_CAR and HANDICAPPED to the enum and edits fits, so ordinal order stops meaning size and the nearest-spot code breaks.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can one spot be both EV and accessible? Does a handicapped permit live on the vehicle or the driver? Is the 95 percent rule per floor or global? Is EV charging billed separately?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Nothing to stop; this is a design change. I keep the old behaviour as the default so existing tests stay green.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Size is no longer the only dimension, so the enum is the wrong place. A second dimension is needed: spot attributes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Write the three new rules as failing tests first (EV takes normal spot, car refused EV spot at 80 percent, allowed at 96 percent).
  5. Root cause (design): The enum was a mild one-way door, as I said when I chose it.
  6. Fix: Keep VehicleType for size. Add EnumSet<SpotFeature> on Spot (CHARGER, ACCESSIBLE) and needs: Set<SpotFeature> on the request. Spot.fits(request) checks size and features.containsAll(needs). The "do not waste an EV spot" rule goes into SpotStrategy (a new FeatureAwareSpot), which can see occupancy. ParkingLot, Ticket, PricingStrategy do not change; a charging fee is a new PricingStrategy decorator.
  7. Prevention: The strategy is covered by tests parameterised on occupancy.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not create EVCar extends Car: charging is a spot concern, not a vehicle behaviour. The cost of attributes is a slightly more general fits.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just add enum values? -> ordinal comparison encodes "bigger fits smaller"; EV is not bigger than CAR, so the invariant breaks.
  • The 95 percent rule needs occupancy; where does it come from? -> A per-type counter (LongAdder) read by the strategy, not a scan.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added HANDICAPPED as a fourth size and spent a sprint patching every ordinal comparison.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: edits the enum and fits.
  • Hire: separates size from features and keeps the lot unchanged.
  • Strong hire: also places the occupancy rule in a strategy and names the one-way-door reasoning.

questions.contextHtml:
An inherited ParkingLot.park is 180 lines. Excerpt:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Ticket park(String plate, VehicleType v, String mode) {
    Spot chosen = null;
    if (mode.equals("NEAREST")) {
        for (Spot s : spots) if (!s.taken && s.fits(v)) { chosen = s; break; }
    } else if (mode.equals("TIGHT")) {
        for (Spot s : spots) if (!s.taken && s.fits(v) && (chosen == null || s.type.ordinal() < chosen.type.ordinal())) chosen = s;
    } else if (mode.equals("LIFT")) { /* 30 more lines */ }
    ...
    double fee = mode.equals("WEEKEND") ? rate * 1.5 : rate;   // pricing mixed in
}
fun park(plate: String, v: VehicleType, mode: String): Ticket? {
    val chosen = when (mode) {
        "NEAREST" -> spots.firstOrNull { !it.taken && it.fits(v) }
        "TIGHT" -> spots.filter { !it.taken && it.fits(v) }.minByOrNull { it.type.ordinal }
        "LIFT" -> TODO("30 more lines")
        else -> null
    }
    val fee = if (mode == "WEEKEND") rate * 1.5 else rate     // pricing mixed in
    ...
}

Every new rule from product is another else if, and a bad merge last month broke weekday pricing.
questions.promptHtml: Refactor it. Which classes appear, which pattern, and how do you migrate safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Splits the method into private helpers inside the same class; still edit-to-extend, still untestable in isolation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is mode global or per request? Which modes are actually in production today? Are there existing tests to pin behaviour?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add characterisation tests that call the old park for each mode and record results before touching the code.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Two axes are mixed: spot choice and pricing. Both vary independently, so two Strategy interfaces. The mode string is a smell of an open/closed violation.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the characterisation tests after each extraction step; compare old and new on a recorded day of entries.
  5. Root cause: Behaviour variation modelled as data flags inside one method.
  6. Fix: SpotStrategy.pick(spots, v) with NearestFreeSpot, TightestFit, NearLift; PricingStrategy.fee(v, duration) with HourlyPricing, WeekendPricing(base) as a decorator. ParkingLot takes both by constructor and does only claim, ticket, map. mode becomes a one-time wiring decision.
  7. Prevention: A review rule: no String mode switches in domain classes; each strategy unit-tested with a fake spot list.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More small classes and a slightly bigger wiring step. I would not add a factory or plugin system until a second team needs to add strategies.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Pricing depends on time of day, spot choice on occupancy: how do strategies get that data? -> Pass a small read-only context (clock value, counters) as arguments; do not give strategies the lot.
  • Strategy count is now 6; wiring is messy? -> A ParkingLotFactory.build(config) is then justified.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Weekend pricing and spot choice were edited in the same if ladder by two people in the same week; a merge dropped one branch.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: private-method extraction only.
  • Hire: two strategies, constructor injection, tests first.
  • Strong hire: decorator for weekend pricing, characterisation tests, and explicit statement of what not to build yet.

questions.contextHtml:
The in-memory lot works for one building. The company now runs 60 lots on a shared service with 4 app instances behind a load balancer, 12 entry gates per busiest lot, peak 3 entries per second per lot. After launch the audit job reports duplicate spot assignments:

audit 14:02  lot=42  spot=117  tickets=[T88213 (KA01AB1234), T88220 (KA02CD9876)]  entered 14:01:58.402 / 14:01:58.431
audit 14:07  lot=42  spot=9    tickets=[T88301, T88304]
instances: app-1 handled T88213, app-3 handled T88220

The team says "the code uses AtomicBoolean, so it is thread-safe".
questions.promptHtml: Explain why it is still broken and how you redesign the claim.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add synchronized" (a lock per JVM does not span four instances), or "use a distributed lock" without thinking about a simpler primitive.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where does state live now (per-instance memory)? Is there already a database? Can one lot's traffic be routed to one instance? What is the acceptable assignment latency?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route all requests for a lot to one instance (hash on lot id at the load balancer), which restores single-JVM semantics while I fix the design. Reversible.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Each instance holds its own AtomicBoolean copy, so CAS is atomic only inside a JVM; two instances both see the spot free. Less likely: clock skew (the 29 ms gap is real concurrency, not skew), a retry from the gate creating two tickets.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare instance ids on the duplicate tickets (different instances, confirmed above); check whether spot state is loaded at startup.
  5. Root cause: An in-process atomic is not a cross-process atomic. The race is the same check-then-act, moved one level up.
  6. Fix: Move the claim into the database as a conditional update and use the rows-updated count as the winner:
UPDATE spots SET taken = 1, ticket_id = :tid
 WHERE lot_id = :lot AND spot_id = :spot AND taken = 0;
-- rows updated = 1: I own it. 0: someone else did, pick the next candidate.

The strategy still only suggests candidates (read free spots from a cache), the DB decides. Add a unique index on (lot_id, ticket_id); release with UPDATE ... SET taken = 0 WHERE ticket_id = :tid AND taken = 1 so a double exit updates 0 rows. 7. Prevention: The audit query as an alert (taken spots must equal active tickets); a concurrency test against the real DB with 40 clients on 5 spots. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not reach for Redis locks or ZooKeeper: the conditional update is simpler and has no lease expiry problem. Cost: a DB round trip per entry, fine at 3 per second per lot. Sticky routing is a stopgap, not the design, because an instance failure loses the in-memory state.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Hot lot at 30 entries per second? -> Partition candidate spots per gate or floor so gates rarely contend; still the conditional update as the arbiter.
  • Claim succeeds but ticket insert fails? -> Do both in one transaction; or a reaper frees spots with no ticket after a timeout.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The same bug appeared in a seat-booking service after it was scaled from one pod to three; the fix was one WHERE taken = 0 clause.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "synchronized" or "it is already atomic".
  • Hire: sees per-JVM scope and uses a conditional DB update.
  • Strong hire: also gives the mitigation by routing, release semantics for double exit, and the audit invariant.

questions.contextHtml: The entrance board shows "Car spots free: 14". A security guard sees the lot is full. Metrics from the lot service: park rate 5/s, scan of 2,400 spots on every board refresh, board refreshed every 200 ms by 6 screens, p99 of park is 340 ms at rush hour (was 40 ms). Next week the free counter is added as a plain int incremented in park and decremented in unpark; after 2 weeks the board shows -3.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: what happened, what is the right design for the "free per type" counter, and what do you add so it cannot drift again?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scanning is slow, so use a counter" and then a plain int incremented from many threads, which creates the drift.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the board allowed to be slightly stale (a second)? Is the counter per type or per floor? Do spots go out of service?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap refresh to once per second and compute the board from a cached snapshot; recompute the counters from the truth (taken flags) nightly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 6 screens x 5 refreshes/s x 2,400 spots = 72,000 reads per second competing with park, which is the p99 regression. (b) counter++ and counter-- from several threads lose updates (read-modify-write), which is the negative number. (c) Increment placed before a failed claim, so failed parks still count.
  4. How I'd verify each: Profile park under the refresh load; a stress test that asserts counter equals the number of taken spots after 100,000 random park/unpark operations.
  5. Root cause: A derived value computed by scanning on read, then cached in a non-atomic variable that is updated outside the action that changes the truth.
  6. Fix:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
private final EnumMap<VehicleType, LongAdder> free = new EnumMap<>(VehicleType.class);
// on successful CAS claim:  free.get(s.type).decrement();
// on release after remove(): free.get(t.spot.type).increment();
int freeFor(VehicleType t) { return free.get(t).intValue(); }   // O(1) for the board
private val free = VehicleType.values().associateWith { java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder() }
// on successful CAS claim:  free.getValue(s.type).decrement()
// on release after remove(): free.getValue(t.spot.type).increment()
fun freeFor(t: VehicleType) = free.getValue(t).toInt()

Update the counter only after the CAS succeeded and only after the atomic ticket removal returned non-null, so each real transition counts once. Note that a bike parked in a car spot decrements the counter of the spot type, not the vehicle type. 7. Prevention: A reconciliation job that logs and corrects any difference between counters and a scan; alert if drift is non-zero; the stress test in CI. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: LongAdder reads are not a perfectly consistent snapshot, which is fine for a sign; I would not use it for the claim decision, that stays with CAS. I would not lock park to keep the counter exact.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why LongAdder over AtomicLong? -> Under heavy write contention it stripes updates across cells; here contention is low, so either works, and AtomicLong is simpler and exact on read. Say which and why.
  • Spot taken out of service for maintenance? -> A third state; decrement the free counter on that transition too.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A board showed 14 free for a full garage for a week; the root cause was a counter incremented on the exit gate's retry path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: plain int counter.
  • Hire: atomic counter updated at the transition, stress test.
  • Strong hire: finds the read-load regression with the arithmetic, adds reconciliation and drift alerting.
